analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from trading individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill never received so much as a committee hearing and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependents from owning or trading individual stocks, bonds of private issuers, futures, commodities, or derivatives that mirror them. They would have 90 days to sell or place these assets in an independently managed blind trust, though widely held index funds, Treasury securities, state and local bonds, and the federal Thrift Savings Plan would remain allowed. Members would certify compliance to the ethics office, which would post the certificates online, and the Justice Department could sue violators for civil penalties of up to $50,000.
analysis.who_benefits: The public, which currently cannot know whether a lawmaker's investment choices are informed by information from their official work. Rank-and-file members who already keep their holdings in index funds would also gain from a level playing field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, and members who already avoid trading

how_it_helps.text: Bars members, spouses, and dependents from owning or trading individual securities, security futures, commodities, and synthetic derivatives, the assets where a lawmaker's official knowledge could most easily translate into personal profit [S2][S3].

Gives members 90 days to divest by sale or by placing holdings in a blind trust whose trustee cannot share information with them and cannot have a close personal or business relationship with them [S2][S3].
Requires each member to certify compliance and makes those certificates public online, so voters can check who is following the rules [S2][S3].

Allows the Attorney General to sue willful violators for civil penalties up to $50,000, paid with personal funds only — not office budgets or campaign accounts — and strips the tax deduction for losses on violating trades [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would have to sell off individual stocks and similar holdings within 90 days or put them into blind trusts they no longer control. Wealth managers who handle those accounts would lose some of that business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The maximum civil penalty is $50,000, which is small relative to many members' wealth, and enforcement depends on the ethics office spotting violations of a self-certification system [S3].

A spouse who receives financial instruments as compensation for their own job gets extra time to divest, an exception a critic could argue softens the ban for households where both partners work [S3].
A trustee of a blind trust has up to six months to sell off assets placed in the trust, so full divestment is not immediate [S3].

A good-faith objection to any trading ban is that disclosure rules already require members to report trades within 45 days, and supporters of the existing approach argue a ban is unnecessary or overbroad; this bill would answer that by going further than disclosure, but the objection was never tested in a hearing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on a few hundred federal officeholders and their households, while the benefit is a clear rule removing a well-known conflict of interest between lawmakers' investment decisions and their official responsibilities. The main design weaknesses are the modest penalty and reliance on self-certification, which a future Congress could strengthen. On balance the trade-off favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither ever took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick introduced the bill on April 28, 2023 together with Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Matt Gaetz, and Raja Krishnamoorthi, pairing a Republican and leading Democrats from opposite ends of the party spectrum [S1][S3].
Seven members cosponsored the bill in total, four Democrats and three Republicans [S4].
The Speaker referred it to the House Administration Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, splitting jurisdiction between the committees that handle ethics rules and tax law [S1][S5].
Neither committee held a markup or hearing, no version was ever brought to the House floor, and the bill died without a vote when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their families, who keep the right to trade individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives while serving, unchanged from before the bill was filed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and their families

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Matt Gaetz, and Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced, giving it Democratic and Republican backing.

for.name: Three additional Democrats and three additional Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, keeping the bill's support bipartisan.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 28, 2023 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for its tax provisions and took no recorded action on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought any member stock-trading ban to the House floor during the 118th Congress, despite multiple bipartisan bills on the issue.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 7 cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans, and the bill was introduced jointly by a Republican with a progressive Democrat, a hardline Republican, and a moderate Democrat — but the obstruction came from committee inaction rather than a recorded vote, so no roll call shows how members would have lined up.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their families
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to sell individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives or move them into blind trusts within 90 days, removing their ability to trade on information their official positions give them. The bill's death leaves that ability intact.

Firms that manage individual stock accounts for member households would have lost some of that business, though the bill still required professionally managed blind trusts and allowed index funds and Treasury holdings, so some fee business would remain.
